Chapter on Bodhi (10a), Treatise, Volume 38,
Chapter on Bodhi.
This refers to the fifth of the five categories of training and the seventh of the seven dharmas.
"Bodhi" means awakening.
In this chapter, the meaning of *bodhi*—the fruit and virtue—is extensively elucidated; it is called *bodhi*.
Third, the mind is explained;
fourth, the enumeration is presented.
The five unsurpassed [qualities].
Regarding the unsurpassed bodhi explained here:
having realized true reality and manifested great supernormal powers, one accomplishes the welfare of both oneself and others.
There must be a fruit as proof;
therefore, this chapter follows after the Chapter on Accomplishment (*Siddhi*).
Within the text, there are three parts.
First, the essence of bodhi is elucidated by means of five gates.
Second, the discourse is concluded with an exhortation to understand it.
Third, at the end of the chapter, three lines praise bodhi.
The text of the first five sections consists of five parts:
first, defining the essence of bodhi by way of wisdom and abandonment, which is termed its "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva);
second, distinguishing bodhi by way of its preeminence.
Third, awakening is distinguished by means of recollecting the merits of the ten titles;
fifth, awakening is distinguished by means of the qualities of differentiation and so forth. These constitute the three [sections] preceding and following [the central one].
First, it is categorized according to the two wisdoms and two abandonments;
next, according to the three wisdoms and two abandonments;
and third, according to the shared and unshared virtues.
Regarding the statement that "the two abandonments and the two knowledges are called bodhi," Tai says:
Just as the nine abandonments and knowledges are called "knowledge" because they are the fruit of knowledge.
The two types of abandonment are also called *bodhi* because they are the fruit of *bodhi*;
thus it is termed *bodhi*. Cè says:
The question is, *bodhi* is defined as awakening (*jñāna*).
The substance of the two kinds of unconditioned [phenomena] is not awakening;
how, then, can they be called bodhi?
The explanation says:
Just as in the tenth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which describes the excellence of the three bodies and the excellence of wisdom, here too it is the same:
both wisdom and abandonment are termed "wisdom."
The reason for this is that within True Suchness (tathatā), all the qualities as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are fully present;
accordingly, it can give rise to the various gateways of merit, such as the wisdoms produced through cultivation.
Therefore, it is called "awakening" (*bodhi*).
It is not because of the illumination of conditions that it is named awakening.
Thus said the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
There is the primordial wisdom of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) which takes the principle of equality as its object;
this is precisely what the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* refers to as "only suchness" (*tathatāmātra*).
That which possesses the wisdom of "only suchness" is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Now, the Tripitaka Master says:
"This explanation is not correct.
The true suchness (tathatā) revealed by the twofold emptiness of persons and phenomena is not the substance of consciousness."
How is it able to illuminate?
To say that "it is like illumination" and "it is like wisdom," and to name this the Dharma-body (dharmakāya),
means that by citing wisdom, True Suchness (tathatā) is revealed and named the Dharma-body.
It is not that the suchness which is identical with wisdom is itself called the Dharma-body.
As for the "two wisdoms," these refer to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons and the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena.
Among the three wisdoms and two abandonments, the first lists the names of the three wisdoms and two abandonments.
"Those who have forever destroyed all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies" refers to the severance of the afflictive hindrances. "Those who have forever and completely severed,
without remainder, the non-defiled ignorance in all its aspects" refers to the severance of the cognitive hindrances.
This refers to the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
In the second sequential interpretation, only the three knowledges (*trijñāna*) are explained, while the two abandonments are not.
Cè (Cèlun) says:
The severance of the afflictive obstructions along with their habitual tendencies is called "pure wisdom," which is precisely the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Because it severs all non-afflicted ignorance regarding all phenomena, it is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajña*).
This is precisely the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Regarding the term "unimpeded wisdom," there are two interpretations.
One says:
Because the functions of the aforementioned two types of wisdom are agile, it is called "unimpeded wisdom" (*asaṅga-jñāna*).
One interpretation states that "unimpeded" refers specifically to the meaning of the agility of the function within subsequent attainment wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
There is no separate entity.
What are called "all afflictions" refers to the one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions and the twenty secondary afflictions.
Regarding the phrase "along with all habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*):

the old [translation] states that because the seeds of the gross *anuśaya* (latent afflictions) have been severed, there remain residual habitual tendencies which are the seeds of the subtle category.
This explanation is incorrect.
Regarding what is now called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*):
because it consists of the seeds of afflictions, the lack of functional capacity within the body is also termed a "tendency.
It is neither identical to nor different from the body composed of the five aggregates.
Because they lack a separate substantial entity, they cannot be said to be different;
because the five aggregates do not cease even after the coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya-vāsanā*) have been severed, they cannot be said to be one.
This is called "habitual tendency."
Regarding the term "omniscient one" (*sarvajña*),
according to various sūtras and śāstras,
the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*).
According to the sūtras and śāstras translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha,
that which is called "wisdom as it is" (*yathāvad-jñāna*) is termed "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because the dharma-realm of true suchness (tathatā) is the causal condition for all dharmas,
it is called "all-seed wisdom" (sarvākārajñatā);
this name is derived from its object.
As the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya states:
"The knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) extinguishes all darkness.
If conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) were called 'all'..."
Now, based on this text:
wisdom that takes the ultimate as its object is called "pure wisdom," while wisdom that takes the conventional as its object is called "all-encompassing wisdom."
Within the context of shared and unshared virtues, there are generally two approaches.
The first concerns maturation based on the person:
this refers exclusively to the merits accomplished by the Buddha-body.
The two vehicles cannot be said to possess what is "unshared.
As stated in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, regarding the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics and so forth:
if these are achieved in common with the two vehicles, they are described as "shared."
As it is said therein regarding the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge of aspirations (*praṇidhijñāna*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),
and so forth: secondly, according to the scriptural exposition,
those qualities of the Buddha taught equally in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings are called "common virtues" (*sādhāraṇaguṇa*).
This refers to the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, and so forth.
If these qualities of the Buddhas are taught only within the Mahāyāna and not in the Hīnayāna, they are termed "unshared" (asādhāraṇa).
As in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises, there are the twenty qualities such as the most pure wisdom (*viśuddhatama-prajñā*).
Furthermore, according to the "Chapter on Qualities" (*Guṇa-parivarta*) of the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra*,
the one hundred and eighty unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of the Tathāgata are elucidated.
As explained extensively therein,
regarding the second point— distinguishing bodhi by means of the seven "supremacies" (*paramatā*)—
what was formerly termed "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) is here termed "supreme."
The terms "supreme" (*parama*) and "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) mutually explain one another:
it is because it is unsurpassed that it is supreme,
and it is because it is supreme that it is unsurpassed.
However, according to the meaning of the Sanskrit original, "most excellent" (parama) is appropriate.
Within this, there are four parts;
first, the enumeration and praise of its excellence.
Second, listing the seven names;
third, explaining according to the names;
fourth, providing alternative explanations for the names.
Regarding the excellence of the basis (*āśraya*), its former name was "the unsurpassed body.
In the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, it is stated that even the enlightenment of the śrāvakas is attained based on an incomplete [basis].

The enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas may be attained based on any body, up to and including a body endowed with thirty-one marks; there is no case where it is attained based on a body fully endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Only the Buddha’s bodhi is designated as having a superior basis because it relies upon a body adorned with the thirty-two marks.
Regarding the four perfections:
the threefold restraint is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because one is free from wrong views, it is called the perfection of view (*dṛṣṭi-saṃpanna*).
Because one possesses the proper deportment of walking, standing, and so forth, it is called the perfection of conduct (*ācāra-saṃpanna*).
Because one is free from wrong livelihood, such as improper begging and preaching for gain, it is called the perfection of pure livelihood (*ājīva-saṃpanna*).
Regarding the abiding in the most excellent state, two chapters are established at the outset.
The first chapter concerns that in which all Tathāgatas predominantly abide;
the second chapter concerns the three unsurpassed and peerless abidings.
In the commentary that follows, first the names of the three dwellings (*vihāra*) are listed.
Second, under the heading "It should be known," the second chapter of the formal exposition is explained first.
Then, under the heading "Within these three dwellings," the first chapter is explained in turn.
Regarding the statement that the three gates of emptiness and the meditative absorption of cessation are called "noble abodes" (*āryavihāra*):
only those that are exclusively noble abodes receive the designation "noble abode.
Therefore, it clarifies that the Tathāgata dwells in the practice of the three gates of emptiness and dwells in the meditative absorption of cessation.
The four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are of the nature of the heavens and are the causes for birth in the heavens.
Because the Buddha abides in these causes for the heavens, they are called "abidings of the heavens" (*devasthāna*).
Although humans may attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because they do not receive the retribution of that concentration, it is not called an "abiding of humans."
The four immeasurables open the path to the Brahma realm and result in rebirth as a Brahma; thus, they constitute the primary dwelling for Brahma.

Among the noble dwellings, those who frequently abide in emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—if they abide in wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), they will grow weary of and renounce dependence on others.
If one dwells in the signless, one rejoices in the ultimate reality;
now, by dwelling in emptiness, one eliminates both aversion and attachment.
If one enters the meditative absorption of cessation, all objective referents and mental activities come to rest.
In the lower three dhyānas, concentration is predominant and wisdom is slight;
in the four formless attainments, concentration is predominant and wisdom is slight;
only in the fourth dhyāna are concentration and wisdom equal, and it is here that the Tathāgata dwells most frequently.
Among the four Brahma-vihāras, the Tathāgata’s mind dwells predominantly in great compassion (mahākaruṇā) because it encompasses suffering.
The following explains the intent of dwelling in great compassion during the six periods of day and night,
as taught in Nāgārjuna’s *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding the addition of one Buddha-abode to the previous three to constitute four Buddha-abodes:
this refers to the Śūraṅgama Samādhi of immeasurable scope, as well as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), and so forth, all of which are Buddha-abodes.
Alternatively, they are divided into ten.
There are eight abodes of the gods,
namely the four of the form realm and the four of the formless realm.
There are four Brahma-abodes,
which are the four immeasurables;
there are four noble stages.
Because there are the wishless [samādhi], and so forth,
up to the attainment of cessation, there are sixteen;
in detail, they are immeasurable.
As stated in that treatise,
regarding the third section which distinguishes the ten titles, Ji says:
"The ten titles are called 'merits to be recollected' (anusmṛti-guṇa)."
Because one attains merit in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings, it is called "merit of recollection.
It is said that the essence of the World-Honored One is singular, yet possesses ten titles.
For now, according to the judgment of the Tripiṭaka masters, the last one among these ten is the general title, while the preceding nine are specific titles.
Among the [twelve] alternative names, the first three pertain to both self-benefit and benefit for others;
the middle three pertain solely to self-benefit;
and the final three pertain solely to benefit for others.

If that is so, while the first and third [statements] clarify only that there is no false cognition regarding phenomena and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), where is it clarified that there is benefit?
To say "there is no falsehood" is not a principle that stands alone; words must have a recipient who receives them.
Therefore, one should know that within "coming" there is also "benefiting others," and so forth; this may be understood by analogy.
Furthermore, it can be understood by inference that within "purely benefiting others" there is also "benefiting oneself.
This interpretation is acceptable.
If one follows the former Master Yuan,
regarding the nine distinct titles,
the first five are names based on his own virtues.
Next are the four epithets concerning the benefit of others.
Since one ought to benefit others,
why speak of one's own virtues?
Furthermore, within the first five [stages], each constitutes two pairs:
the former manifests the perfection of the Path, while the latter contemplates the ultimate limit of cessation.
The third clarifies the perfection of the two causes—initial quiescence and insight—followed by the single excellence of the fruit.
Now, speaking according to the meaning of the term:
"responding" (ying) carries only the sense of responding to benefit;
it does not mean benefiting others.
Therefore, it is also for one's own benefit.
Cè (Cèlù) says:
"In this way, there are seven ways in which these ten titles are so named."
The term *Tathāgata*, *Arhat*, and *Sugata* are names derived from causes;
*Samyaksaṃbuddha* is a name derived from both function and essence;
and *Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna* is a name derived from qualities and the ultimate meaning.
The "Knower of the World" (Lokavid) and the "Teacher of Gods and Humans" (Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām) are named according to their object and their function.
The "Unsurpassed Charioteer of Men" (Anuttara-puruṣa-damya-sārathi) is named according to the person [he guides] and his function.
"Buddha" is named according to its essential nature.
The name "Bhagavat" is established based on multiple meanings;
namely, the six meanings such as "sovereignty" (īśvara) and so forth, as explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
One who is called "Tathāgata" because they are devoid of falsehood is [meant here].
The old treatise states:
"It is not because there is something that exists as it is spoken of that he is called the Tathāgata.
If one follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhìdù lùn) or the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chéngshí lùn), it says: [as follows].
Because one comes by means of the path of reality as it is to achieve perfect enlightenment, one is called a Tathāgata.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Because one comes by means of the six pāramitās and the eleven kinds of emptiness, one is called a Tathāgata."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"Because he comes riding upon the *prajñāpāramitā* to transform sentient beings, he is called the Tathāgata.
The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
Because he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, he is called the Tathāgata.
Question: If it is said that one who is without falsehood is called the Tathāgata, [then...]
The Buddha originally made a vow based on causes and conditions:
"If sentient beings do not enter nirvana, I shall likewise not enter;
if sentient beings do not attain bodhi, I shall likewise not realize it."
Although he has made this vow, sentient beings do not enter nirvāṇa of their own accord nor attain bodhi;
yet the Buddha would abandon sentient beings to personally enter nirvāṇa and realize bodhi.
"How can it be said that names and words are not false?
Master Jing replied,
"This principle is also difficult."
One explanation states that although this vow exists in the initial arousal of the mind, from that point onward,
even though the bodhisattva observes that they benefit others, it does not equal that of a Buddha.
If one does not attain Buddhahood, the benefit of others will not be extensive;
therefore, it is necessary to realize the path to Buddhahood.
However, as long as sentient beings have not entered the remainderless state, one shall ultimately never enter nirvana without remainder oneself.
Therefore, there is no falsehood.
Furthermore, it is said:
"When the root mind is first generated, one vows to deliver all sentient beings, swearing that one will not realize *bodhi* until they have done so."
Now, although these bodhisattvas have accomplished the practices of the ten stages, they do not take realization [as their final goal],
as in the case of Mañjuśrī and others.
As it says in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:
There are two types of icchantikas:
first, those who have severed their roots of goodness;
second, bodhisattva-icchantikas who ultimately do not take up unsurpassed enlightenment.
Regarding the term "Samyaksaṃbuddha" (Perfectly Awakened One), Cè states:

this takes the wisdom of the fundamental nature (*mūladharmatājñāna*) as its essence; furthermore, it is called "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*) because it takes the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdhajñāna*) as its essence.
Now, this shall be explained:
it may also be that correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is called "right awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*),
while subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*) is designated as "awakening" (*bodhi*).
Regarding the statement "as it is in the ultimate sense" (*paramārtha*):
the reality of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is collectively termed the ultimate,
because it is contrasted with the phenomena that exist only as imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
It is taught that the dependent nature is also called the ultimate truth.
"Knowledge" refers to the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*).
"Practice" is as explained in the sūtras.
Regarding the two chapters on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as the old treatise states:
"The three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*) are as explained in the sūtras;
one practices the two dharmas of the chapters on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*."
The present treatise reverses that [conception].
They are called the "three clear knowledges" (tisro vidyāḥ) because they counteract ignorance regarding the three time periods.
It is asked:
Ordinary persons, learners (*śaikṣa*), arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all buddhas alike know the past.
For what reason is there the distinction between "clear knowledge" and "not clear knowledge," or "power" and "not power"?
The answer is:
Ordinary persons and those still in training merely have a general knowledge of the fruits;
because this knowledge is subject to exhaustion, it cannot be called "clarity" (vidyā).
This applies to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those who are fully endowed [with these qualities].
The Buddhas' simultaneous knowledge and illumination of all causes and effects, such that their understanding of phenomena is exhaustive, is called "clarity" (*vidyā*).
As for what occurred eighty thousand kalpas ago, it lies beyond the reach of ordinary penetration; thus, there remains a lack of knowledge.
Being constrained by this lack of knowledge, it cannot be termed "power" (*bala*).
Question: Regarding the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*),
ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles alike know eighty thousand [kalpas].
For what reason is it said that the divine eye sees the present:
that ordinary beings see the four continents, the Brahma kings see a small chiliocosm, the śrāvakas see a medium dichiliocosm, and the pratyekabuddhas see a great trichiliocosm?
Jingyun: The functions of wisdom within the five consciousnesses of the divine eye and divine ear are inferior;
therefore, they perceive at varying distances according to the strength of one's vital energy.
The present objects are separated by spatial boundaries, and one perceives them at varying distances according to one's capacity.

Regarding the supernormal knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*) and others, it is known through the power of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that they can extend as far as eighty thousand [kalpas].
There is an explanation [to this effect].
Only those of the bodhisattva lineage can know eighty thousand eons as being unborn,
such as the Sāṃkhyas and others do;
this is not the case for other ordinary beings.
In the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 100, the distinctions between the views of eternalism and the kalpas remembered are explained:
those of the śrāvaka lineage remember twenty thousand kalpas,
while those of the pratyekabuddha lineage remember forty thousand kalpas.
The bodhisattva lineage recollects eighty thousand kalpas;
within the "Exposition of the Teacher of Gods and Humans," the initial enumeration is presented as chapters, which are further explained according to their meaning.
Because it opens the way to the explicit meaning;
because it is explained as the true eye;
and because it serves as the basis for all meanings.
The term "explanation" (*vyākhyā*) is used because it constitutes actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Since the meaning (*artha*) is manifested based upon wisdom, it is that which wisdom relies upon; thus, it is the "basis of meaning.

Regarding the fourfold analysis—such as "the common [meaning] is not fully understood, while [this explanation] is that which brings about full understanding"—it is called "actual meaning" (*bhūtārtha*) because it constitutes the true significance.
First, the Tathāgata is able to provide definitive resolution regarding meanings that sentient beings have not yet understood.
Second, he is able to sever the meanings that arise in common with sentient beings.
Third, he is able to reveal the profound depths of the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) shared [with them].
The fourth [point], "together with the initial realization of the profound," is for the purpose of making it even more luminous and pure.
Because it possesses these four meanings, it is said to be "for the sake of the true meaning" (*tattvārtha*).
The three phrases beginning with "because it is the root of all phenomena" explain why it is "the true dharma" (*dharmatā*).
"Dharma" refers to the teaching.
This is because the Tathāgata shares the teaching as his fundamental basis with all beings,
and because he acts as the guide who reveals the teaching.
Because he serves as the basis for the teaching, the Tathāgata is the True Dharma. The preceding section clarified the virtues of the teacher;
the following explains the meaning of "teacher."
The Tathāgata is able to correctly instruct and grant guidance to devas, humans, and others.
[Master] Ce (Cè) says:
"That which is called the 'true eye' refers to the wisdom that takes conditions as its object."
"For the sake of true knowledge" refers to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
"For the sake of true meaning" reiterates the knowledge of meaning (*arthajñāna*).
"For the sake of true phenomena" reiterates the knowledge of phenomena, and so forth.
Regarding the three categories, such as the collection of dharmas that lead to and encompass meaningful benefit,
the old treatise states:
"beneficial in meaning, not beneficial in meaning, and neither beneficial nor non-beneficial in meaning."
This refers to the three natures, such as the wholesome and so forth.
He who possesses many virtues capable of destroying all māras is called Bhagavat;
according to the tradition of the Western Regions, this title signifies "Most Victorious."
Whether they be non-Buddhists or followers of the Buddha’s teaching, all praise their own teacher as Bhagavān.
Since there is no equivalent name for this term in the Chinese language, the Sanskrit term has been retained.
This is according to the Sanskrit original.
The beginning of all sutras states "The Bhagavat," without using the term "Buddha";
likewise, at the end, there is no title of "World-Honored One" (Lokanātha).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*:
To claim that one is called "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) because of possessing the aforementioned nine virtues is also not consistent with reason.
Fourth, in the section explaining the manifestation [of the Buddha], there are three parts to the text.
First, it is clarified that within a single world-system, there may be many kalpas without a Buddha appearing, or there may be a single kalpa in which many Buddhas appear.
Second, from the passage "In each and every [direction]" onwards, it is clarified that there are immeasurable Buddhas in the worlds of the ten directions.

Third, it is definitively established that there is not a single buddha-field in which two buddhas appear; this clarifies the intention that within a single world-system, no two buddhas appear simultaneously.
Regarding the preceding section, there may be cases where multiple buddhas appear within a single eon.
Thus, within this Bhadrakalpa, one thousand Buddhas appear.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"When the world was first formed, there was a thousand-petaled lotus flower in the great ocean."
Even as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, they saw a cluster of water containing a thousand lotuses, and they exclaimed:
"In this kalpa, a thousand Buddhas will appear; it is an auspicious and excellent age."

Question: If the thousand Buddhas appear together within a single kalpa of formation and destruction, why does Paramārtha state that no Buddhas appear during the kalpas of formation, destruction, or emptiness, but only during the kalpa of abiding do Buddhas appear in the world?
Within twenty kalpas, Buddhas appeared in the world during the first ten kalpas,
but not during the latter ten.
Within the first ten kalpas, Buddhas also did not appear during the first five kalpas.
In the sixth kalpa, Krakucchanda Buddha appeared in the world;
in the seventh kalpa, Kanakamuni Buddha appeared in the world;
and in the eighth kalpa, Kāśyapa Buddha appeared.
Śākyamuni appeared during the ninth kalpa;
Maitreya Buddha will appear during the tenth kalpa.
Following Maitreya, for immeasurable kalpas, there shall be no Buddhas appearing in the world.
Thus we know that the thousand Buddhas do not appear across multiple cycles of formation and destruction;
if there are a thousand Buddhas in the Bhadrakalpa,
it is said they all exist within a single kalpa of formation and destruction.
Furthermore, there were a thousand Buddhas during the past *kalpa* of Adornment (*vibhūṣaṇa-kalpa*).
They too should have been within the same single *kalpa* of formation and destruction;
yet, if one says they were identical [in time], that is not so.
As it is said in the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bhaiṣajyasamudgata-sūtra*:
The Buddha addressed the great assembly,
"In the past, I encountered the Buddha Prabhāsa."
At the outset, upon hearing the names of the fifty-three Buddhas, his heart was filled with joy;
he immediately proclaimed them to others,
and a thousand people resolved their minds [upon enlightenment].
Passing it on again,
another thousand people resolved their minds on Bodhi;
thus, through successive instruction, another thousand people resolved their minds on Bodhi.
The first thousand sons of good family are none other than the thousand Buddhas of the past Adornment Eon;
the middle thousand are none other than the thousand Buddhas of the present Auspicious Eon.
The latter thousand [Buddhas] will appear in the world during the future Nakṣatra Kalpa.
Just as among those past Buddhas of the Adorned Kalpa,
the last three Buddhas— namely, Vipaśyin Buddha— appeared in the world during the first of the ninety kalpas.
Just as the Buddhas Śikhin and Viśvabhū appeared in the world during the thirty-second kalpa,
after which there were no Buddhas until the ninety-first kalpa, which is the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Kalpa).
Thus, Krakucchanda Buddha first appeared in the world;

This is not the path of true purity;
the path of true purity is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
In the thirteenth section on "not giving unsuitable objects," there is a presentation, an explanation, and a conclusion.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, one does not inform others, nor does a bodhisattva perform [the act]," Kibi says:

This refers to a case where, for example, there is someone who has previously not eaten onions and does not inform others of this fact; yet, according to the principle of giving, they share it with another, and the bodhisattva does not do so.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Not only is this onion not to be given to them,
but one should also not give to them any other articles that are unsuitable for their vessels or inconsistent with their ritual observances and various activities.
This is the intended meaning here.
Furthermore, one should not give to a bodhisattva by tossing the gift up and down;
nor should one give to a bodhisattva while maintaining improper deportment.
Master Ji says:
Regarding the phrase "or else placing [them] in [certain positions]," this refers to,
for instance, placing another person in a position where they must perform improper acts before one then practices giving.
For example, giving after having caused others to kill and so forth.
Regarding the fifteenth [type of giving], which is not practiced for the sake of fame or profit, there are four sub-clauses.
The twenty-sixth [verse] states:
"Appropriate to the time and not inappropriate to the time" means,
for example, giving food when one is hungry rather than giving clothing,
or giving cooling things when it is hot rather than giving fire.
Regarding pure giving for oneself and others:
this refers to not perceiving a giver or a receiver,
while remaining in accordance with the proper ritual.
The meaning of giving those things such as knives, poison,
or alcohol with an undisturbed mind can be understood.
This concludes the twenty-ninth [section] on the practice of giving for the increase of wisdom.
First is the general introductory statement;
second is the detailed explanation through question and answer;
and finally is the conclusion.
The extensive explanation contains four sections of text.
In the third section, it says: "Those whose nature is fixed in stinginess and greed are of the class of stingy and greedy persons.
This means that having a naturally stingy and greedy disposition is what is called being "by nature stingy and greedy."
If one is not inherently stingy and greedy, but becomes so through the instruction of others, they belong to the category of those who are stingy and greedy by influence.
In the fourth section, it says: "One still conceals their own faults so as not to let others know them, let alone provoke them."
How much more so when one is present before them and awakens them through speech!
The preceding section clarifies the existing gift of material wealth;
the following section clarifies the existing gift of non-material wealth, which is divided into two parts.
First, it correctly explains the practice of giving that increases wisdom even when one currently possesses no wealth;
subsequently, it determines the stage,
identifying this as the practice of giving by a "provisionally named" bodhisattva prior to the [first] bhūmi.
This is not the stage of entering the grounds (*bhūmi*).
Second, in the explanation of the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*),
first the distinction between giving and not giving is established with reference to physical scriptures and so forth.
Second, how is it that a bodhisattva employs skillful means regarding non-giving? This is a repeated explanation through question and answer concerning the skillful means of practicing giving.
Within the preceding section, there are two parts;
first, distinguishing between the giving and non-giving of scriptural volumes.
This means that if there are fellow students of the Buddha-Dharma who seek out a scriptural volume, a bodhisattva should assess himself:
if he has already mastered the meaning of this sutra, he should give it to them;
if he has not yet understood it himself and must still study it, he should not give it away.
The second section clarifies the absence of physical scrolls and so forth, which consists of three statements regarding the observation of one's own mind.

In the first two of these statements, it says: "Even if, by means of this practice of giving the Dharma, I were to [fail to attain anything], how much less could I possibly cause a deficiency in the provisions for sublime wisdom?"
Tai said:

"Suppose that because of this dharma one becomes dull-witted and mute, unable to endure the faults of the afflictions of stinginess regarding the Dharma; even in such a case, one should still practice the gift of Dharma.

How much more so when, at the time of giving the Dharma, because one lacks it oneself, one causes those present to be deprived of the provisions for sublime wisdom—would one not then be dull-witted and mute, unable to give?"
Now, examining the old treatises, it says:
"I would rather give the gift of Dharma even if it results in being foolish and mute in this present life, so as to eliminate afflictions;
how much more so when it serves as the skillful means for producing wisdom in the future?"
Within the third phrase, there are again three reflections.
Regarding the statement, "Is it for the sake of harming one's own afflictions? and so forth, this means:
"Is it for the purpose of harming one's own afflictions that one practices the gift of Dharma?"
Should one practice the gift of Dharma in order to fulfill the provisions for one's own wisdom?
Rather than giving away such scriptural volumes and other materials of the provisions for wisdom to others,
it is superior to retain the original texts and read them oneself, thereby increasing the provisions for wisdom.
It is not that giving to others produces this merit;
rather, giving scriptures to others does not yield such benefit.
It is only for those who, though currently meager in the benefits of the Dharma, possess awakened wisdom, that [this gift] is truly beneficial.
If one neglects one's own study and recitation to give away scriptural volumes to others,
one will only fail to obtain abundant benefits of the Dharma and awakened wisdom in future lives.
This is the second question and answer, which provides a further explanation regarding skillful means.
Regarding the statement "as with a bhikṣu’s pure relinquishment," there is both indirect pure giving and direct pure giving.
As stated in the Vinaya,
the third [section] clarifies the giving of the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Jing says:
In this context, it refers to preaching the Dharma to others with full comprehension of the names and essences of the three kinds of giving;
that is, the peerless practice of giving both the Dharma and its meaning.
If one understands the principles of the distinctions between cause and effect, one may preach according to the inclinations [of others].
This is called the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Being well-versed in local dialects and exhorting others to practice the three kinds of giving constitutes the unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Tái says:
As for the alternative classification (*paryāya*):
giving with a portion of compassion is called an alternative classification.
One should know, as they truly are, the essential nature of giving, the etymological explanation of the term "giving," and the causes and effects of giving.
This is called the "unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence" (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Master Ji, citing the Tripiṭaka, states:

"If one explains the etymology, essence, and characteristics [of this] through various methods, this constitutes the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena and meaning (*dharma-artha-pratisaṃvid*)."
Because it involves the analytical discernment of many different categories regarding the signifier and the signified;
if there is a distinction between cause and effect, this constitutes the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*),
because it analytically explains causes and effects.

Furthermore, if one follows the concluding text below, which simply states "by means of material giving" and "by means of the Dharma," this would conclude the two preceding sections by means of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) without specifying which analytical knowledge it is.
Why is it not said that all four types of unimpeded knowledge (pratisaṃvid) are subsumed?
To explain this now:

it is said that among the aforementioned three—giving material wealth, giving the Dharma, and giving fearlessness—all their various aspects constitute the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid).
This means that the various teachings of the Dharma mostly analyze the characteristics of phenomena through diverse methods.
If the essence and the characteristics were identical, there would be no impediment to their meaning;
however, the meanings expressed therein mostly refer to the "essence" (svabhāva) by way of the actual substance, while referring to the "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa).
If it refers to the explanation of names, it is called the unimpededness of etymological interpretation (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), because it explains the meanings of words and characters.
If it refers to the distinction between cause and effect, it is the unimpededness of analytical exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Because it is able to discern the causes, effects, and phenomena of the Dharma,
all four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) are contained herein;
for these unimpeded knowledges exist in relation to the giving of material wealth and so forth.
To practice giving while knowing it as it truly is is called the gift of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, within each of the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge, there are various gateways, essential characteristics, and even [the analysis of] causes and effects.
It is not necessarily the case that they are assigned separately.
Now, according to the old treatises,
one should compare their characteristics and, if necessary, distinguish them by name and meaning, cause and effect.
Thus, it is an excellent explanation to take the various synonyms for the foundation, such as the "unimpeded knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) and so forth.
Fourth, the immeasurable giving of the mind is explained:
the phrase "those who have been kind" and so forth refers to the mind that relinquishes attachment to kin.
Fifth, the explanation of the giving of antidotes.
This section has two parts:
first, a general presentation, and second, a detailed explanation.
In the detailed explanation, there are three parts.
First, the four obstacles to be remedied are clarified;
second, the four wisdoms that serve as the remedies are clarified.
The subsequent section clarifies that there are distinctions in the functions of the four wisdoms.
Cè states:
"As for the nature of the four obstacles..."
First, it consists in the lack of functional capacity within the seeds due to not having been previously cultivated;
second, it is the scarcity or deficiency of material things to be given,
if one discusses external objects.
Because the six dharmas and four characteristics constitute the objects of the senses.
As for the internal factors and so forth,
they take the five aggregates and twelve links as their essence.
Third, attachment to excellent, delightful, and agreeable material objects,
which has predominant greed as its essence.
Fourth, the deep longing and delight upon observing the future fruition of abundant wealth.
It takes wrong view that seeks future fruits as its essence.
Next, the four wisdoms that serve as the antidotes are explained.
The first is "awakening."
First, awakening oneself:
although one has not habituated to giving in the past and possesses abundant wealth, one practices giving with diligence rather than taking pleasure in it.
Second, enduring various sufferings.
First, one who is able to give away suddenly what was originally a small amount of donated goods, enduring the suffering of hunger and cold;
second, one who endures the suffering of poverty;
third, one who thoroughly understands perversion—that which is deeply attached to exquisite wealth as being pleasant and pure.
One causes them to know that these are all the roots of impurity from which afflictions arise;
thus, one is able to extract and abandon them,
which is called knowing perversion.
Fourth, regarding those whose nature of practice through views is not firm:
they do not cling to the fruits of giving, having realized the nature of impermanence.
Sixth, the explanation of giving with superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
The former name was "internal, solitary, pure-minded giving.
Among the difficult practices of giving, it is said that there may be those with "superior merit" (*agrya-adhika*).
The old treatise refers to this as "superior objects of giving" (*adhimātra-dāna-vastu*).
The former Great Virtuous Ones explained it as follows:
"It refers to material objects for offering, such as the seven treasures and so forth.
Now, we rely on the new treatise.
Regarding those who possess superior kindness:
it may be a person of great or profound kindness whom one sends with gifts to bestow upon another;
or it may be one's own children, wife, or slaves, who have been kind to oneself, whom one gives away to others.
It is indeed difficult to explain.
Regarding the four general characteristics within the practice of giving through all gates,
according to the older treatise, there are five sections of text.
The four sections are identical to the New Treatise (Xinlun),
with one additional sentence:
"If one personally collects [the requisites] for giving."
For this reason, the ancients enumerated four gates differently:
parents constitute one,
and wife and children constitute two.
Servants and laborers constitute the third;
virtuous friends and ministers constitute the fourth.
Now, according to the New Treatise:
First is one's own wealth;
second is wealth obtained through transforming others;
third is giving to relatives, parents, and so forth.
There are four types of giving to those who come to one.
The first two are distinguished according to material wealth;
the latter two are distinguished according to the recipient of the gift.
The giving of a virtuous person can be understood through five characteristics.
Within the giving of all kinds, there are thirteen characteristics.
First is the gift that is independent of worldly motives.
That is to say, it does not rely on fame or the karmic retribution thereof.
Second, regarding vast giving:
one does not regard the recipient.
Because all seeking by ordinary beings and sages is empty,
the *Sūtra on Good Precepts* states:
"Do not discriminate between a field of merit and what is not a field of merit."
Giving with joy refers to being joyful during the three periods [of preparation, execution,
and conclusion]. Giving to the five fields of merit refers to giving to the pure field of merit consisting of the four classes of people and the path.
Sixth is giving to those who are not worthy recipients (*akṣetra*).
In the older treatise, the sixth is named "giving everything" (*sarvadāna*).
Seventh is giving all things (*sarvavastudāna*).
This refers to the relinquishing of all things.
There are eight types of universal giving (*sarvatraga-dāna*),
which refer to the specific locations from which one gives.
Ninth is giving at all times,
which means not discriminating against specific seasons or periods.
Tenth is blameless giving.
This refers to giving to others wealth or goods that are not in accordance with the Dharma.
As for "giving to the lands of the twelve directions," it means giving whatever is required according to each respective region.
The older treatise omits the giving of sentient beings and material objects;
it divides wealth into two categories,
thus making thirteen items in total.
Thus, there are eight kinds of seeking for gifts.
The old treatise speaks of "giving to remove affliction.
Briefly stated, there are nine kinds of giving that bring happiness in this world and the next.
Master Ji said:
"For instance, as the former Master Yuan explained,
there are three types each for wealth, the Dharma, and fearlessness."
Regarding the three kinds of wealth,
the first is that which is most excellent and sublime;
the second is that which is pure.
There are three ways of acquiring it in accordance with the Dharma.
"Exquisite" refers to superior objects such as mani-jewels and the like.
"Pure" means that it was not obtained through robbery or theft.
That which is "in accordance with the Dharma" refers to wealth that is in accordance with the Dharma, such as [proper goods], and not things like weapons or alcohol.
It should be understood that there are three types each for the fearless gift of the Dharma and so forth.
Furthermore, some say:
The first refers to the giving of material wealth, the giving of the Dharma, and the giving of fearlessness;
this distinguishes the three types of essence.
Upon these three, there are six functions of the mind.
The gift of material wealth has two functions:
namely, it removes the defilement of stinginess and hoarding.
The gift of fearlessness has three [functions].
This clarifies the three fears.
Giving the Dharma and [giving material things] are combined into one. Question:
In this context, why is it that elsewhere the gift of Dharma is placed first and the gift of fearlessness last,
whereas here the gift of fearlessness is placed first and the gift of Dharma last?
The meaning is as follows:
The treatise below states:
"Material giving and the giving of fearlessness can bring peace and happiness to sentient beings in this life;
for both of these provide happiness in the present."
The reason why the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*) is explained after the material gift (*āmiṣa-dāna*) in immediate succession is that it benefits future lives; therefore, it is explained later.
Tai says:
Subduing stinginess means relinquishing attachment to material wealth.
Even when others know that a certain object is of no use to them,
they still do not give it away because of their stingy attachment to it.
Subduing the accumulation of stores means abandoning attachment to their use.
One accumulates wealth and goods intending to enjoy them for oneself;
the bodhisattva likewise abandons this mind.
Among the three types of giving, the first consists of relinquishing superior and exquisite material wealth;
the second and third consist of non-superior and non-exquisite material wealth.
Pure giving possesses ten characteristics.
Regarding those who do not come seeking but swiftly hope to obtain wealth— just as various bodhisattvas swiftly hope for the bestowing of gifts—
they together swiftly hope for the bestowing of gifts;
when they encounter such a person, they swiftly hope to obtain wealth.

Regarding "not grasping at the giver," the old commentary states that this refers to not holding divergent views, such as the view that clings to [the notion] that emptiness has no fruit and so forth;
there are three such views.
1. The view that there is emptiness where there is no fruit;
2. The view that harming [others] constitutes the true Dharma;
3. The view that what is not supreme is supreme.
These three are all subsumed under false views.
Why is this? If one follows the Sarvāstivāda school:
To view what is not superior as superior is subsumed under the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Now, according to the Mahāyāna,
the grasping of views must be a conceptual image of a view in order to be designated as such.
In this context, because they do not take views as their object, these are not "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

Furthermore, when one who seeks—whether individually or collectively—sees [the donor] directly, why would they cling to the notion that there is a difference between the gradual giver and the immediate giver, given that the objects [given] are equal?
That is to say, if one were to give to a hundred people individually and sequentially,
or if one were to give all one hundred at once simultaneously,
the merit would be equal.
For what reason do you maintain that merit has distinctions?
Regarding the fortieth fascicle, the Chapter on Precepts (Śīla-varga), there are three titles according to the Sanskrit original.
*Śīla* is translated here as "cooling" (*qingliang*).
This clarifies that the essence of the precepts possesses a supreme power capable of rendering the practitioner’s body and mind cool and refreshing.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *vinaya*, which is translated as "discipline" (*tiaofu*).
According to the teaching, this refers to those who are capable of subduing.
Furthermore, there is another term, *vinīta*, which in this region is called "already subdued.
This refers to those who practice the Vinaya and are thus termed "already subdued."
In the Sanskrit original, there are only these three names, and the term *vinaya* does not appear.
If one says that "discipline" (*lüyí*) and "precepts" (*jiè*) are both local [Chinese] names,
Jing says:
Because it involves restraint and prevention, it is called "precept" (*śīla*).
Precepts encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
each, whether wholesome or unwholesome, possesses its own form of restraint and prevention.
Now, it is explained that "precept" (*śīla*) is so named because virtuous precepts prevent and ward off unwholesome dharmas.
If one were to say that it is called a "precept" because it prevents what is wrong and stops evil,
then how could "unwholesome precepts" (*duḥśīla*) be said to prevent what is wrong and stop evil?
Because of this obstacle, it can be said that what is called "prevention" (śīla) is also termed "restraint" (saṃvara).

That which internally harmonizes is called "restraint," while that which externally manifests in accordance with the proper method is called "discipline" (vinaya). Although discipline applies to both wholesome and unwholesome precepts, here we clarify wholesome discipline.
Master Ji said:
"Precepts are another name for the prevention of wrongdoing.
As for what is called 'evil precepts' (duḥśīla)..."
The nature of evil is not śīla;
evil in relation to śīla is called "bad śīla" (duḥśīla).
If that were so, then the nature of evil would likewise not be view (dṛṣṭi).
It is called "wrong view" (mithyādṛṣṭi) because it emerges from what is evil;
this interpretation is not correct.
When one seeks [the meaning] through its etymological root, both the wholesome and the unwholesome are equally subject to investigation.
Purity is termed *śīla*.
*Śīla* seeks to eliminate the nature of evil.
The preceding "Chapter on Giving" (*Dāna-paṭala*) has already explained the removal of external stinginess.
Now, this chapter follows because one maintains the precepts to guard against internal defilements.
Within the text, there are three parts.
First the inquiry, next the explanation, and finally the conclusion.
Within the explanation there are again three parts;
first, the explanation of the ninefold pure precepts.
The second [section] clarifies the benefits of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The third clarifies the functions of ethical discipline.
Within the first [of these], the initial verse and its prose commentary set forth nine topical headings.
Subsequently, the analysis according to the gates consists of nine sections.
Within the explanation of the self-nature (*svabhāva*), there is first the question, next the explanation, and finally the conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are three parts.
First, the enumeration and listing of names;
second, the sequential explanation;
third, the summary of the benefits and the resolution of difficulties.
Among the four types [of precepts], those obtained through cultivation based on others are called "right reception from another.
Those not based on a teacher’s bestowal, but consisting of a vow for one's own purity, are called "excellent purification of mental action" (*manas-karma*).
As the Old Treatise says:
To receive the precepts with a well-purified mind and immediately repent after committing an offense is called "returning to purity.
To be consistently cool and pure is called "profound respect and single-minded mindfulness.
Regarding the explanation, there are three parts: the first two concern receiving [the precepts], and the latter two concern maintaining them.

First, based on the two types of undertaking (*samādāna*), three points are established according to their sequence: first, the explanation of undertaking in accordance with its differentiation; second, the explanation of original purity and subsequent purification.
Within the former, regarding the original undertaking, one says in relation to others: "I am able to uphold [the precepts]."
Therefore, when one now commits an offense against others, one feels shame;
and because one originally vowed that "I shall never again violate the precepts," one feels self-reproach.
Regarding the statement that one is free from all evil actions due to two causes and conditions,
Tai says: first,
receiving them correctly from another.
Second, because the purity of intention serves as the causal condition, one does not give rise to regret later.
There are four interpretations regarding this by [the master] Ce.
The first says:
the two types of sensation constitute one condition, and the two types of maintenance constitute another condition.
The second says: [the same].
Thus, the two types of restraint serve as the two conditions.
Third, it says:
shame and remorse serve as the two causal conditions, while the two types of feeling serve as the two conditions.
Fourth, regarding the two types of restraint:

although there are many interpretations, [it is held that] the two types of volition (*cetanā*) serve as the two causes, while shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) serve as the two conditions.
Now, taking these two types of retention as the two conditions is an interpretation that accords with the textual phrasing.

Within the concluding praise of the benefits, one should understand that this refers to the sublime, virtuous, pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), its correct reception (*samādāna*), and its subsequent training (*anuśikṣaṇa*).
In terms of the morality of restraint (saṃvara-śīla),
it should be understood that this comprises the immeasurable pure precepts and all other precepts that encompass wholesome qualities.
It should be understood that this refers to the ethical discipline of gathering sentient beings (*sattvasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*), which benefits all sentient beings and so forth;
it should be understood as the pure ethical discipline (*viśuddha-śīla*) that is capable of attaining great fruits and supreme benefits.
In summary, the three precepts yield great fruits and benefits.
Among all the precepts, there is first the question, followed by the explanation, and finally the conclusion, which introduces what follows from what precedes.
Within the explanation, there are two parts.
First, all precepts are briefly explained in relation to both the laity and the ordained;
second, from "Furthermore, based on this... onwards, all precepts are explained in detail.
Within this [second section], there are two further parts.
First, it clarifies that the essence of the three clusters of precepts (*tri-saṃvara-śīla*) is that which is to be studied.
Second, under the section beginning with "All bodhisattvas who wish [to train] in such bodhisattva training," it clarifies that training in reliance upon the precepts is the act of studying.
The preceding section has three parts:
first, a brief clarification of the three clusters of the precept-essence within the undertaking;

second, from "How does a bodhisattva abide in the restraint precepts and abide in the precepts for gathering virtuous dharmas? onwards, an extensive clarification of the characteristics of the three clusters of precepts within the maintenance.
The third [section] concludes it.
Within the preceding [section], there are two parts;
the first is a general restatement of the opening.
Second, the detailed explanation according to the chapters.
Regarding the statement that "the sevenfold prātimokṣa discipline received by bodhisattvas is precisely the bhikṣu precepts and so forth," Jing says:
The bodhisattva vow extends far as far as enlightenment.
Now, when identifying a bodhisattva based on the formal observances (vinaya) of the seven classes of practitioners,
it is because their regulation of gross transgressions is the same.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva exists within the seven classes of followers.
Regarding the seven branches of body and speech, they may or may not be complete depending on those seven classes.
Among them, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs possess the seven branches of body and speech.
For the five groups—the śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās—there are only the four branches of body and speech;
however, they all fully possess the three [branches] of mind.
The bodhisattva, moreover, possesses the great precepts.
The two assemblies possess ten factors;
the remaining five assemblies have only seven factors, excluding the three from speech.
Furthermore, although Bodhisattvas may outwardly belong to the latter five assemblies, [they still possess all ten].
Nevertheless, because they are fully endowed with the abandonment of all evils,
when members of the seven assemblies receive the vows of discipline, they all possess the ten paths of wholesome action,
as they have distanced themselves from every form of evil.
Because all such virtues are cultivated and all such births are subsumed [within it].
Ce (Cesheng) states:
"The essence of the bodhisattva vows and the śrāvaka vows is indeed distinct."
However, when those among the seven assemblies who have previously received the śrāvaka precepts later receive the bodhisattva precepts, the branches and seeds that arise are as follows:
if they are bhikṣus, they are like the branches and seeds of the bhikṣu precepts.
Excluding those factors not shared with the śrāvakas,
the remaining categories of factors are identical to those generated by a bhikṣu.

Furthermore, when male or female lay followers (upāsaka/upāsikā), having completed the reception of the five precepts, subsequently receive the bodhisattva precepts, the categories of factors generated are identical to those of the lay precepts.
Therefore, it is said that these seven kinds of precepts are themselves the bodhisattva’s discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).

Although one may receive them without generating the [bodhisattva] resolve, they are said to be the very same precepts received by the seven classes of practitioners simply because their constituent factors and types are identical.
The remaining bodhisattva precepts—the four pārājikas, the forty-two light offenses, and so forth—are all included within the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
These various precepts are established because there are transgressions within the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
This is not the morality of restraint;
furthermore, one loses the śrāvaka precepts but does not lose the bodhisattva precepts.
The reason for this is as follows:
Upon the death of a śrāvaka or the arising of both sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana), one loses the śrāvaka precepts but does not lose the bodhisattva precepts.
Alternatively, there are two conditions for loss:
first, loss through the regression of the bodhicitta.
Second, there is the fault of giving rise to increased afflictions,
yet one does not lose the śrāvaka precepts; thus,
one knows the distinction between the bodhisattva precepts and the śrāvaka precepts.
Regarding the statement in the *Śīlasaṃvara-sūtra* concerning "all that [is undertaken] for the sake of great enlightenment" after a bodhisattva has received the vows of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*),
this is a brief summary.
Jing says:
In reality, the principle of receiving the three clusters of precepts is simultaneous; however,
they are explained as sequential in meaning,
because one first abandons evil and subsequently practices what is good.
Ce said: "According to the old treatise, it means that when a bodhisattva receives the vows of restraint (saṃvara-śīla),
the people of former times explained it as follows:"
Comparing the former with the latter,
their superior discipline and correct intention are identical; yet, for these reasons,

It is called "superior" because it encompasses the cultivation of wholesome qualities that are not shared with the two vehicles.
When it is now said, "after receiving the vows of restraint," this refers to the sequence of stages according to the meaning.

The commentary states:
This explanation clarifies the characteristics;
the precepts of restraint (saṃvara-śīla) constitute the goodness of cessation.

Because it clarifies the characteristics of cultivation once one abides in pure morality,
it is said that "undertaking the vows of restraint for the sake of great enlightenment is called the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas."
This is because, in terms of ultimate reality, it is taught that one receives all three clusters of precepts simultaneously.
How this is so will be explained extensively below;
therein are three parts.
First, the inclusion of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*) is clarified by means of the three types of wisdom (*tri-vidyā*).
Second, it is clarified by means of the three types of action (*tri-karma*);
thus, at each respective time, bodily action (*kāya-karma*) is elucidated.
Regarding "toward all sublime objects," the following clarifies verbal action (*vākkarman*).
Regarding "in the realms of the ten directions," the following clarifies mental action (*manaskarman*).

Regarding "with body, speech, and mind," the following summarizes the three types of action to clarify the practices of dedication, making vows, and offering, while remaining free from negligence in physical action (*kāyakarman*).
First, the three [types of merit] are explained with reference to the field of respect (*gurukṣetra*).
Following the section on "sickness," they are explained with reference to the field of compassion (*karuṇākṣetra*).
Third, following the section on "the various rules of training" (*śikṣāpada*), if one follows Jing’s commentary, the seven types of goodness (*saptakuśala*) are explained.
Now, according to [the commentary by] Cè, it clarifies the nine wholesome factors:

Third, right practice;

The meaning is as follows:

the first two constitute "sameness of purpose" (samānārthatā).

As previously cited separately, furthermore, among the [four] means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), there is that of sharing in common (*samānārthatā*) which involves shared pleasure and pain; it is pleasant at first but painful in the end.
This should be sought according to the text.
Next, regarding the first aspect of loving speech (*priyavāditā*),

the passage beginning with "by means of corresponding phrases and so forth" up to "and thus proclaims it," clarifies the characteristic of teaching according to the principle (*yathārtha-deśanā-lakṣaṇa*) by means of seven points.
First, by way of corresponding phrases;
second, by way of companions;
third, by way of conformity.
Fourth, it is pure and lofty;

The seventh is the method for dividing the provisions of the constant application (*nitya-prayoga*).

These various phrases are explained in detail in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (顯揚聖教論), the "Section on the Compendium of Explanations" (*Vyākhyāna-saṃgraha*), and so forth.
In the "Section on the Compendium of Explanations," it asks: what constitutes the "text" (*vyañjana*)?
There are six kinds:
first, the collection of names (nāmakāya);
second, the collection of phrases (padakāya).
Third is the body of letters;
fourth is speech;
fifth is the mode of activity.
Sixth is the request by the audience.
As it says below, "one should know that speech possesses eight qualities in brief," namely:
being excellent at the beginning, beautiful, and so forth.
By means of the correspondence of those words, phrases, and so forth, up to the provisions consisting of constant and diligent application, one is able to preach the True Dharma.
Thus, these eight aspects of speech, categorized into three groups, briefly possess the three virtues.
First is the quality of orientation,
which refers to the first type;
second is the quality of intrinsic nature.
That is to say, the next two types.
Third is the virtue of application (prayoga-guṇa),
which refers to the remaining types.
"Correspondence" (yoga) refers to the fact that the sets of names, phrases, and syllables are well-established in their proper sequence;
furthermore, it refers to correspondence by way of the four kinds of reasoning.
"Accompaniment" (sahāya) refers to that which can establish the sequence.
"Conformable" means that it explains the sequential order;
"lucid" means that the phrasing is clear and distinct;
and "pure support" means that it skillfully enters the minds of the multitude.
It is "congruent" because it is like the assembly,
because it is worthy of offerings,
and because it accords with the Dharma.
Because it draws out the meaning and because it accords with the proper time.
